title: Merge two messy restaurant listings
summary: Generate two inconsistent listings of the same fictional restaurants, merge them into one deduplicated catalogue, and explain every match and every non-match.
context: Plateful is a fictional food-discovery app that buys restaurant listings from two vendors. They describe many of the same places differently: abbreviations, a missing pin code, flipped word order, a branch listed as its own restaurant, a closed place one vendor never removed.

You do not have their files, so you generate them. Start from about 300 fictional true restaurants, write a seeded generator that adds noise to produce the two listings, and keep the answer key apart from the merge code.
Then build the merge. Wrongly merging two places is worse than missing a duplicate: a customer sent to the wrong branch has a bad day.
must_have: The generator, its seed, and the two listings it writes, with at least five distinct kinds of noise.
A merge that outputs one catalogue with a stable id per restaurant, the source records behind each, and a stated rule for every field where the vendors disagree.
A stored explanation for every pair considered: which fields agreed, which differed, the score and the threshold.
An evaluation against the answer key: precision, recall, and the worst wrong merges and missed merges listed.
A review queue: borderline pairs go to a file for a human instead of into the catalogue.
nice_to_have: Blocking, so ten times the records does not mean every pair is compared; state the effect on recall.
Branches modelled as children of a brand, neither merged nor treated as duplicates.
A note on what would change at five million records.
constraints: No paid services, APIs or accounts, and no geocoding or maps API. Free open-source packages only.
Fictional data only: restaurant names, owners and phone numbers are made up, and numbers are obviously non-working. Real locality names are fine.
deliverables: A public repo created after you press Start, with commits spread across the window.
A README with how to run everything (regenerate the data, run the merge and the evaluation), your results, and what is missing.
judge_focus: How you chose the threshold, and what cost you decided a wrong merge carries.
Whether an explanation would convince a sceptical reader, including for a pair you got wrong.
Whether the evaluation is honest about the generator's noise being easier or harder than real vendors' files.
A trail of commits: a crude matcher first, measured, then improvements justified by the failures.
bengaluru_context: Data and catalogue teams at Bengaluru food-delivery, local-search and maps companies spend much of their year on entity matching like this, where the cost of a wrong merge is measured in complaints.
